newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU harmonised price data show smaller differences.
newsitem.headline: EU harmonised price data show smaller differences.

text.p: The European Commission issued harmonised inflation data for European Union countries on Friday showing smaller differences in inflation rates across the bloc as it prepares to introduce a single currency.
The harmonised indices showed all countries except Greece had year-on-year rates in January below three percent.
EU countries will be judged early next year on whether their 1997 finances have converged enough to join economic and monetary union (EMU). Price stability is one of five criteria.

"We continue to think that the all EU members except Greece will be able to qualify in 1997 for the inflation criterion," said economist Theodor Schonebeck at Deutsche Bank research after seeing the new figures..
Economist Ellen van der Gulik at JP Morgan took a similar line. "It is very likely that most countries are going to make this criterion," she said.
Van der Gulik said the most striking thing with the harmonised figures was that they were much less divergent between countries than the ones published nationally.

"The inflation rates based on harmonised inflation are much closer together which will make it easier to meet the criterion given that it is a relative criterion, it is relative to the best performing member states," she said.

According to the EU's Maastricht treaty, a country's average inflation rate observed over a year before joining EMU should "not exceed by more than 1.5 percentage points that of, at most, the three best performing member states in terms of price stability".
The harmonised figures showed some countries with significantly different rates than previously published by national statistics agencies.

For example, Sweden's harmonised inflation figure amounted to 1.3 percent compared with the nationally published figure of a fall of 0.1 percent and Britain's harmonised rise was 2.1 percent compared with the increase of 2.8 percent reported nationally.

The harmonised data, worked out in cooperation between the EU's statistics agency and national statistics offices, showed that Finland, Sweden and Luxembourg had the bloc's lowest inflation rates in January -- 0.9 percent, 1.3 percent and 1.3 percent respectively.
Greece, Portugal and Spain had the highest rates -- 6.6 percent, 2.8 percent and 2.8 percent respectively.
The EU inflation rate was 2.2 percent compared with 2.7 percent a year earlier. -- Brussels newsroom +32 2 287 68 11
